name: Rust-Sacrament
geological_features: Dry lake beds with evaporite deposits
specific_features: Microbial communities that accelerate iron oxidation, literally rusting the planet
Dust devils of red oxide particles that persist for days in low gravity
description: Rust-Sacrament is a small desert world stained entirely in shades of red and brown by the iron oxide that constitutes the bulk of its surface material. The planet is actively rusting, not merely through chemical weathering but through the metabolic activity of microbial communities that catalyze iron oxidation at rates far exceeding abiotic processes. Every surface is coated in fine red dust, every cliff face streaked with the darker browns of more advanced oxidation, and the atmosphere itself carries a perpetual red haze of suspended iron oxide particles that turns the sky from horizon to horizon into a dome of dried blood.

The thin atmosphere supports spectacular dust devil formations, columns of red oxide particles that spiral upward for kilometers in the low gravity and persist for days, wandering the surface like restless spirits. The dust is incredibly fine, penetrating even sealed environments and coating everything in a rust-colored film that requires constant maintenance to manage. Temperatures swing between extremes, the iron-rich surface absorbing heat efficiently during the day and radiating it just as rapidly at night, the thermal cycling generating mechanical weathering that feeds fresh iron to the microbial oxidizers.

The iron-oxidizing microbes represent one of the most successful planetary-scale biological processes ever documented, their combined metabolic activity having transformed the surface chemistry of an entire world. The organisms are present in every sampled environment, from the deepest accessible subsurface layers to the atmospheric dust particles themselves, each population adapted to its specific niche but all performing the same fundamental chemistry: converting reduced iron to rust and deriving metabolic energy from the reaction. The dry lake beds contain evaporite deposits that record the planet's transition from a wetter world where the microbes first evolved to the arid state that their own activity helped create by consuming atmospheric oxygen.

Iron ore extraction from Rust-Sacrament requires no mining in the traditional sense, as the surface material is already oxidized to compositions that require minimal processing for industrial use. The hematite is of excellent grade, and the evaporite minerals include valuable industrial chemicals. The primary challenge is the dust itself, which infiltrates and damages equipment at rates that make maintenance the dominant operational cost. The microbes are of scientific interest as examples of biology that has reshaped an entire planet's chemistry, a living lesson in the power of simple processes repeated across geological time.
